concept.name: SQL Query Tuning: Index Seeks, Scans, Clustered & Covering Indexes

relationships.description: Database indexing establishes core B-Tree vs LSM-Tree mechanics; SQL query tuning applies B-Tree seeks, scans, and covering index structures to optimize production relational queries.

SQL covering indexes achieve sub-5ms latency inside the database engine without cache invalidation complexity, whereas in-memory caches achieve sub-millisecond QPS at the cost of external RAM and cache-aside state management.
Sharding distributes tables horizontally across instances, but single-node partition performance remains fundamentally governed by clustered and covering index design.

spark.summary: SQL query tuning and indexing reduce disk I/O and CPU scans from O(N) full-table reads to O(log N) B+tree lookups and covering index-only scans using execution plans and selectivity statistics.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always measure with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before adding indexes: a single well-ordered composite index (equality columns first, range/sort columns last) routinely cuts p99 latency from seconds to single-digit milliseconds without bloating write amplification.

concept.whyItMatters: At 10M+ rows, a missing or poorly ordered index forces sequential heap scans that saturate NVMe IOPS, evict shared buffers, and stall connection pools under concurrent OLTP load.
whenToUse: High-selectivity WHERE predicates (< 5–10% of rows) on large tables in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, or SQL Server.
Hot JOIN keys, ORDER BY / GROUP BY clauses, and pagination queries where avoiding an external disk sort cuts latency by 10x–100x.
Read-heavy endpoints that can be satisfied entirely from an index via covering columns (INCLUDE) without touching heap pages.
whenNotToUse: Tiny lookup tables (< 1,000 rows or a few 8 KB pages) where a sequential scan is faster than traversing B+tree levels.
Low-cardinality boolean or status flags (e.g., is_active = true matching 95% of rows) unless paired with a partial index (WHERE is_active = false).
Write-saturated append-only ingestion tables where every extra secondary index adds B+tree page splits, WAL volume, and vacuum overhead.
keyPoints: B+tree composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: place high-selectivity equality (=) columns first, then range (>, <, BETWEEN) or sort (ORDER BY) columns.
Covering indexes (CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (col)) enable Index-Only Scans in PostgreSQL when the visibility map confirms all-visible pages, eliminating random heap fetches.
Query planners rely on ANALYZE histograms and pg_stats (n_distinct, most_common_vals); stale statistics cause nested-loop vs. hash-join misestimates.
Non-sargable predicates like WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' or WHERE created_at + INTERVAL '1 day' > NOW() defeat standard B+tree indexes unless backed by an expression index.
Unused or duplicate indexes silently degrade INSERT/UPDATE throughput; audit pg_stat_user_indexes (idx_scan = 0) before creating new ones.

examples.title: PostgreSQL 16 multi-tenant order pagination
examples.scenario: An e-commerce API runs SELECT id, total_cents, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND status = 'PAID' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 on an 80M-row table, using only single-column indexes on tenant_id and created_at.
examples.outcome: Replacing both with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_status_created ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_cents) switches the plan from Bitmap Heap Scan + Top-N Heap Sort (1,420 ms, 48,000 shared buffer reads) to an Index-Only Scan (1.8 ms, 5 buffer hits).

examples.title: Partial index for unprocessed outbox events
examples.scenario: A Spring Boot service polls a 25M-row outbox table with WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 every 200 ms, while 99.9% of rows are already published.
examples.outcome: Creating CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_pending ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL shrinks the index from 1.9 GB to 4 MB, keeping it pinned in shared_buffers and dropping poll latency from 310 ms to 0.4 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Each targeted B+tree or GIN index turns multi-second table scans into sub-millisecond point or range lookups.
tradeOffs.con: Every INSERT, UPDATE on indexed columns, and DELETE must update all affected indexes, generating extra dirty pages, WAL bytes, and HOT-update disqualifications.

tradeOffs.factor: Composite covering indexes vs. storage footprint
tradeOffs.pro: INCLUDE columns satisfy queries with Index-Only Scans, avoiding random 8 KB heap page reads.
tradeOffs.con: Wider index tuples reduce B+tree fanout, increase tree depth, and consume more RAM in shared_buffers or InnoDB buffer pool.

tradeOffs.pro: GIN accelerates JSONB/full-text containment (@>) and BRIN tracks min/max per 128-page range at 1% of B+tree size for time-series data.
tradeOffs.con: GIN has expensive pending-list flushes on heavy writes, and BRIN degrades to full scans if physical rows are not correlated with insertion order.

failureModes.name: Parameter sniffing / plan instability
failureModes.description: A cached generic plan built for a rare tenant_id (10 rows, Nested Loop) is reused for a whale tenant (2M rows), causing CPU spikes and timeouts.
failureModes.mitigation: Use pg_stat_statements to spot high variance, force custom plans when needed (plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan), or partition skew-heavy tenants.

failureModes.name: Stale planner statistics after bulk loads
failureModes.description: Loading 5M rows without running ANALYZE leaves pg_class.reltuples outdated, tricking the optimizer into choosing Nested Loop joins over Hash Joins.
failureModes.mitigation: Run ANALYZE immediately after batch ETL/COPY jobs and tune autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor (e.g., 0.02 instead of 0.1) on large tables.

failureModes.name: Blocking DDL locks during index creation
failureModes.description: Running plain CREATE INDEX acquires a SHARE lock that blocks all concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements for minutes on large tables.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL) or ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE (MySQL) with lock_timeout set to 2s.

failureModes.name: Deep OFFSET pagination degradation
failureModes.description: SELECT ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500000 forces the engine to scan and discard 500,000 index entries on every page turn.
failureModes.mitigation: Switch to keyset (cursor) pagination: WHERE id > :last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 for constant O(log N) latency at any depth.

commonMistakes: Indexing every column individually instead of designing composite indexes matched to actual WHERE + ORDER BY predicates.
Putting a range column (created_at > ...) before an equality column (tenant_id = ...) in a composite B+tree index.
Using SELECT * on OLTP endpoints, which prevents Index-Only Scans and pulls large TOAST/text columns into memory.
Applying functions to indexed columns in WHERE clauses (e.g., DATE(created_at) = '2026-11-12') instead of half-open range bounds (>= '2026-11-12' AND < '2026-11-13').
Testing query plans on an empty or 1,000-row staging database where the planner naturally picks Sequential Scans.

sections.content:
## The idea

SQL query tuning aligns physical storage access paths with how the cost-based optimizer (CBO) estimates selectivity, join order, and I/O cost. Instead of scanning millions of 8 KB heap pages sequentially, you shape predicates to be sargable (search-argument-able) and build balanced B+tree, partial, or specialized indexes so the engine touches only the exact leaf pages and heap blocks required.

## Concrete walkthrough

1. Capture slow queries in production via `pg_stat_statements` sorted by `total_exec_time` and `shared_blks_read`.
2. Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)` on a representative bind parameter to compare `actual rows` vs. `estimated rows`.
3. Spot high-cost nodes: `Seq Scan` with heavy `Rows Removed by Filter`, `Sort Method: external merge Disk`, or `Nested Loop` multiplying a 100x underestimated row count.
4. Rewrite non-sargable expressions into range predicates and eliminate `OFFSET` in favor of keyset cursors.
5. Create a composite covering index `(equality_cols, range_or_sort_col) INCLUDE (select_cols)` using `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
6. Re-run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and verify `Heap Fetches: 0` (after `VACUUM`) and single-digit `shared hit` counts.

sections.content:
## Composite key ordering and sargability

A B+tree stores keys lexicographically. An index on `(a, b, c)` supports predicates on `(a)`, `(a, b)`, and `(a, b, c)`, plus `ORDER BY b` when `a` is constrained by `=`. Once a range operator (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `IN` with many values) appears on column `b`, subsequent column `c` cannot use the tree order for filtering or sorting. Always place equality predicates first, sort/range columns second, and non-filtered projection columns inside `INCLUDE` so they do not bloat internal branch pages.

## Index types by workload

| Index Type | Engine Support | Best Workload | Size Overhead | Write Penalty |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **B+Tree** | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server | Equality, ranges, `ORDER BY`, prefix `LIKE 'abc%'` | Medium (15–30% of table) | Moderate (page splits + WAL) |
| **Partial B+Tree** | PostgreSQL, SQLite | Sparse states (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) | Very Low (1–5% of table) | Low (only matching rows) |
| **GIN** | PostgreSQL | JSONB `@>`, arrays, full-text `tsvector` | High (30–80% of table) | High (pending list / fastupdate) |
| **BRIN** | PostgreSQL | Append-only time-series (`created_at`) | Tiny (< 1% of B+tree) | Negligible |
| **Hash** | PostgreSQL (10+), Memory | Strict `=` on long strings/UUIDs | Medium | Low–Moderate |

## Failure modes

The most deceptive production outage is **planner cliff flipping**: a query runs in 3 ms for months until table growth crosses a cost threshold and PostgreSQL suddenly switches from an Index Scan to a Parallel Seq Scan, saturating disk read bandwidth. Equally dangerous are **HOT update breaks**—adding an index on a frequently updated column like `updated_at` prevents Heap-Only Tuple updates, doubling vacuum bloat—and **index bloat** from heavy churn, which requires periodic `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` or `pg_repack`.

## Observability and verification

Track `pg_stat_statements` weekly for `calls * mean_exec_time` and `shared_blks_read / calls`. Verify buffer efficiency (`shared hit` vs `shared read`) rather than wall-clock time alone, because warm OS page cache can hide an unindexed scan that will fail under cold-cache load. Pair `pg_stat_user_indexes` with `idx_scan = 0` checks over a full monthly billing cycle before dropping redundant indexes.

## Practical checklist

- Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` against production-scale data before writing migrations.
- Order composite B+tree columns as `(equality_cols, range_or_sort_col) INCLUDE (projection_cols)`.
- Replace `OFFSET` pagination with keyset cursors (`WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id)`).
- Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` with `lock_timeout = '2s'` in migrations.
- Keep `pg_stat_statements` enabled and prune unused indexes (`idx_scan = 0`) quarterly.

questions.title: Diagnosing Key Lookup vs Index Only Scan in Execution Plans
questions.prompt: In an execution plan for a query filtering on a secondary index, you observe an Index Seek followed by an expensive 'Key Lookup' (or 'Bookmark Lookup') consuming 85% of total query operator cost. What is the root cause and the most efficient resolution?

options.text: The table statistics are outdated; running ANALYZE TABLE will automatically convert the query to an Index Only Scan without index changes.
options.explanation: Statistics describe data distribution but cannot provide missing column data that is physically absent from secondary index leaf pages.

options.text: The secondary index satisfies the WHERE condition but lacks columns referenced in the SELECT clause, forcing the engine to fetch row data from the clustered index for each matching row. Solution: Add the missing projected columns to the index as key or INCLUDE columns (Covering Index).
options.explanation: Correct! Key Lookups occur whenever a non-clustered index does not cover all columns requested in the query. Expanding the index into a covering index eliminates the lookups.

options.text: The primary key is corrupted; rebuilding the clustered index with DROP and RECREATE will eliminate secondary lookups.
options.explanation: Key lookups are normal behavior for non-covering queries, not a sign of index corruption.

options.text: The database engine has exceeded max_connections and downgraded the execution plan to sequential I/O.
options.explanation: Connection limits affect client concurrency, not optimizer index covering decisions.

rubric.excellent: Identifies that missing projected columns trigger secondary-to-clustered random I/O lookups and prescribes a covering index with INCLUDE columns.
rubric.acceptable: Recognizes that the index is missing columns required by the query.
rubric.gap: Confuses key lookups with table corruption or outdated query statistics.

questions.sampleSolution: A Key Lookup occurs when an index seek satisfies query predicates but fails to provide columns in the SELECT projection. Creating a covering index (CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table (where_cols) INCLUDE (select_cols)) allows an Index Only Scan, dropping I/O to zero heap accesses.
questions.explanation: By storing unindexed projection columns in the leaf level of the index via INCLUDE, the engine resolves the query entirely within the index B-Tree.

interviewProblems.title: Architect High-QPS Multi-Tenant Query Indexing Under High Concurrency
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are the Principal Database Architect for a multi-tenant SaaS ledger processing 10,000 queries per second on a table with 200,000,000 rows. A critical endpoint executes: SELECT transaction_id, created_at, status, amount FROM ledger WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status IN ('PENDING', 'FAILED') AND created_at >= ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50. Currently, the query takes 3,500ms and causes 100% database CPU. How do you design the clustered index, composite secondary indexes, and query structure to guarantee sub-5ms p99 latency?
constraints: Zero downtime allowed during index deployment

dimensions.name: Composite Index Key Ordering
dimensions.description: Applying equality-before-range rules to minimize B-Tree leaf scan volume.

dimensions.name: Covering Index & Key Lookup Elimination
dimensions.description: Eliminating random page reads for projected columns (amount, transaction_id).

dimensions.name: Production Operational Safety
dimensions.description: Zero-downtime online index builds without table write locks.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: 1. Index Design: Create a composite covering index: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_ledger_tenant_status_date ON ledger (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (amount, transaction_id). Leading tenant_id provides exact partition seek. status IN (...) performs bounded range seeks. created_at DESC aligns perfectly with ORDER BY created_at DESC, eliminating in-memory sorting. INCLUDE (amount, transaction_id) satisfies SELECT completely, yielding an Index Only Scan with zero Key Lookups. 2. Operational Safety: Deploy via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (or ALGORITHM=INPLACE in MySQL) to prevent exclusive table locks, avoiding transaction pool starvation. 3. Result: B-Tree depth traversal requires 4 page reads, scanning at most 50 leaf entries, executing in <2ms directly from buffer cache.
commonPitfalls: Placing created_at as the leading column, forcing a scan across all tenants
Omitting amount from the index, causing 50 random Key Lookups per query
Running standard CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY, causing full table write locks

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Sql Query Tuning Indexes

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: SQL query tuning and indexing reduce disk I/O and CPU scans from O(N) full-table reads to O(log N) B+tree lookups and covering index-only scans using execution plans and selectivity statistics.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Composite B+Tree applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Heap & Visibility Map.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Heap & Visibility Map experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use pg_stat_statements to spot high variance, force custom plans when needed (plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan), or partition skew-heavy tenants.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Always measure with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before adding indexes: a single well-ordered composite index (equality columns first, range/sort columns last) routinely cuts p99 latency from seconds to single-digit milliseconds without bloating write amplification.
Avoid trap: Indexing every column individually instead of designing composite indexes matched to actual WHERE + ORDER BY predicates.
Avoid trap: Putting a range column (created_at > ...) before an equality column (tenant_id = ...) in a composite B+tree index.
When to reach for it: High-selectivity WHERE predicates (< 5–10% of rows) on large tables in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, or SQL Server.
When to reach for it: Hot JOIN keys, ORDER BY / GROUP BY clauses, and pagination queries where avoiding an external disk sort cuts latency by 10x–100x.
